title: Sequences, convergence, and divergence
terms: sequence; limit of a sequence; epsilon–N definition; convergent sequence; divergent se- quence; divergence to infinity; oscillation.

exposition.text:
A real sequence is a function a : N → R, written (a ). It converges to L ∈ R if for every ε > 0
n
there is N such that n ≥ N implies |a − L| < ε. The quantifier order matters: N may depend
n
on ε, but must work for every subsequent index. A finite limit is unique, and altering finitely
many terms changes neither convergence nor the limit.
Divergence means failure to converge to a finite real number. The notation a → +∞ means ev-
n
ery real threshold is eventually exceeded; it is a special kind of divergence. Oscillation need not
prevent convergence if its amplitude tends to zero. Conversely, two subsequences with different
limiting values disprove convergence. Identify the size of a term before treating its alternating
sign.

For a = 2 + (−1) /n, what is the smallest positive integer N such that |a − 2| < 1/100 for
n n
every n ≥ N?
(A) 99 (B) 100 (C) 101 (D) 199 (E) 200

solution.text:
The error is exactly 1/n, independent of parity. The strict inequality holds precisely when
n > 100. Thus N = 101 works for the entire tail, whereas N = 100 fails at its first index.

question.text:
n
How many subsequential limits does a = (−1) + 1/n have?
n
(A) 2 (B) 0 (C) 1 (D) Infinitely many (E) 3

solution.text:
Even and odd subsequences tend to 1 and −1. Every convergent subsequence must eventu-
ally approach one of these two values, since its distance to {−1, 1} is 1/n.
